item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I think that leaving the window open would let timeline changes escape the loop to solidify into history as we know it.

That's why the Foundation can be so confident about greenlighting potentially disastrous butterfly-effects; but is so adamant about closing the window in time. To the point that they are willing to lose staff and resources.

Drop a nuke through and enjoy the pretty colors. Close the window in time, no harm done. But leave it ajar when reset hits and all of history is instantly and irrevocably retconned to include the total destruction of Chicago in 1875. Complete with all the fallout (both literal and figurative) that would flow from such a thing. Shaping a new timeline that, for all anyone here and now knows, is the way history always had unfolded.

This SCP would then be about a window that opens to the "Chicago Cataclysm", with speculation that the forces unleashed during the disaster are what caused the window to become lodged at an odd angle to normal time.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
What if they contacted a Foundation from that time and found a time travel anomaly from inside? That way it's not crossing SCPs any more than they would already necessarily have been crossed. It would be interesting to see whether they could escape the loop. They could simulate K-Class events like paradoxes and the repercussions probably wouldn't extend to the real time stream.
If someone looked at simulation SCP-096, would real SCP-096 get angry too?
And I think it did talk about protocol for removing simulation materials from the simulation, so maybe they could take SCP-500 from inside. Except I guess this is the wrong time. And nobody wants an SCP to create an infinite source of that stuff, because that makes everything too easy to be fun. Maybe it would be a neat idea for a tale, to see what Foundation protocol becomes when infinite supplies of those comes.
Or if they look at that observation-based jade sculpture whose number I can't remember; would the real one teleport to kill them when it gets a chance or would they be okay after leaving the simulation?
I guess there are a lot of SCPs that cause remote effects, and most of them pose that question about whether or not real world ones start acting based on simulation ones' circumstances.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
One important thing to remember for experiments, that is easily overlooked, is that the window opens on the third story of a building. So that limits the ease of travel to and from the loop.

I have an issue with the containment logs being too lax. The implication is that leaving the window open could result it the time loop leaking through. That could be more than a minor inconvenience, yet we rely on human action for the safeguard. It would not be much trouble to attach a purely mechanical (since the facility's seem to have semi-frequent electrical problems) device that forces the window shut at the t-90 second mark. Precluding the possibility of override from either side, like in the "My partner is just behind me, we have to wait for him," while aiming a gun at the room cliche, that is not too unlikly, and could cause things to go pear shaped.

+ SCP crossing ahead
- I warned you.

Edit: Since it is stated that it matters not where it is mounted, it could be mounted horizontally. This is a favorite tweak of mine for dimensional portals that seems to be frequently overlooked on this site. (In full disclosue, I have never played that game) Since the Foundation seems not to care about killing people, and/or damaging that 'world', and since the it is a time loop, reactions from that world can be safely predicted, it could be used as a hazardous waste disposal window. SCP-505-1, just as an example. I am not proposing tossing unwanted SCPs out the window, (although SCP-871 at a soup line would probably be welcomed …) but as a way to get rid of tricky byproducts. Particularly the non-anomalous ones, that I can't seem to remember an instance of.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
There's a weird anomaly that's centered in the office of a patent attorney. The purpose of a patent attorney is to make sure you have legal protection for the patent on your new invention.

The last client who went to see the patent attorney (to demonstrate his new invention) before the weird anomaly started… we don't know who he was. The secretary said the client "was peculiar" and smelled strange, and had a strange accent. He didn't have an appointment, he didn't have a visiting card… he just showed up. Like he was unfamiliar with how things are done, or perhaps like he didn't want any record of his name.

This odd-smelling, odd-acting, odd-sounding man shows up at the patent attorney's office in order to demonstrate some odd invention, and then nobody ever sees him or the patent attorney again, and the next morning there's an anomaly centered on the patent attorney's office.

And you don't see any significance?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
"Unwashed" = he smelled odd.

As for the accent — note that the secretary said the man's accent sounded Polack, not that it was Polack. He sounded odd.

And he didn't have an appointment or a visiting card, so they don't know his name. And he showed up to see the patent attorney. That means he had an invention.

This odd-smelling, odd-sounding man had an invention that did something very, very odd. How did it happen? Did he mean for it to happen? Was he even human?

We will never know.
